To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the epidermal and ErbB3 receptors are not expressed in normal human mammary gland epithelial cells but are expressed in breast cancers.

the epidermal (EGF) growth factor receptor (ErbB/HER) family of receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) is the best studied family of RTK and that its members are involved in a number of different types of cancer, including lung, head and neck, breast and ovarian.
the EGFR family of ligands and their receptors are important in tumourigenesis and that their activity can be regulated by the microenvironment, particularly the extracellular matrix.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the EGFR in cancer and the development of novel therapies which target this pathway.
the study of the epidermal and related growth factor systems in normal and malignant cells.

understanding the role of the EGF receptor in normal development, its role as a tumour promoter, the molecular basis of resistance to anti-tumour agents which target this receptor, and the design of novel agents for the treatment of tumours which have acquired resistance to existing agents.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the epidermal system of ligands (the epidermal growth factors, EGFs) and receptors (the EGFRs) is a family of growth factors and receptors which are involved in the regulation of cell growth, differentiation and migration.

the epidermal family is a group of receptors which bind a family of ligands, the binding of which results in receptor dimerisation and autophosphorylation, and the phosphorylated receptor in turn phosphorylates a series of substrates.
this is a complex system which can interact with many other growth factor systems and which can be activated by many different ligands and which can be involved in a variety of cellular responses.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the EGFR family is involved in the control of many aspects of normal development and homeostasis and that the dysregulation of this system is a frequent event in cancer.
the EGFR system has been studied in great detail and is well understood.
the EGFR system is a complex one and that the ligands and receptors are not as simple as we would have liked.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the EGFR family is an important component of a complex system which is involved in many cellular processes.
the EGFR family of receptors and ligands is not a monolith, and that the individual components of the family are not identical, and that this is important in the context of tumours.
the EGFR family is not as simple as it first appeared and the interactions of the ligand-receptor complexes with their downstream signalling pathways are not always as expected.
